\chapter{Chapter 4}\label{appendix:C}
\index{Appendix@\emph{Appendix C}}

\section{Geometry of \texorpdfstring{$\Omega_{\hat{\psi}}$}{Omega\_psi-hat} for Simpson's Index} \label{sec-Omega-psi-hat-geometry}

Recall that for a model with full parameter $\symbf{\theta} \in \Theta$ and parameter of interest $\psi = \varphi(\symbf{\theta})$, the set 
$$
\Omega_{\hat{\psi}} = \left\{\symbf{\omega} \in \Theta: \varphi(\symbf{\omega}) = \hat{\psi}\right\}
$${#eq-omega-hat-psi-general}
is the level set of $\varphi$ at the MLE $\hat{\psi}$. In the multinomial model with $J$ categories, $\Theta = \Delta^{J-1}$, where 
$$
\Delta^{J-1} = \Bigg\{\symbf{\theta} \in \mathbbm{R}^J: \theta_j > 0,\ \sum_{j=1}^J \theta_j = 1\Bigg\},
$${#eq-open-simplex}
the open $(J-1)$-dimensional probability simplex. Taking Simpson's index
$$
D(\symbf{\theta}) = \|\symbf{\theta}\|^2 = \sum_{j=1}^J \theta_j^2
$${#eq-simpson-index}
as the parameter of interest, i.e.\ $\varphi = D$, gives
$$
\Omega_{\hat{\psi}} = \left\{ \symbf{\theta} \in \Delta^{J-1} : \|\symbf{\theta}\|^2 = \hat{\psi} \right\}.
$${#eq-omega-hat-psi-simpson}

Since the level sets of $D$ are intersections of the simplex with hyperspheres, they admit a clean geometric characterization. We will derive this characterization for arbitrary $J$ first, then consider the special cases $J = 2$ and $J = 3$ in detail for some added intuition. While these low-dimensional cases do not produce nuisance parameters of sufficient dimension for the integrated likelihood to produce estimates that meaningfully outperform the profile likelihood, they nevertheless serve as concrete illustrations of the general result.

\subsection{General $J$} \label{sec-general-J}

\subsubsection{Level Set Structure} \label{sec-level-set-structure}

Define the affine hyperplane 
$$
\Pi = \left\{\mathbf{x} \in \mathbbm{R}^J: \sum_{j=1}^J x_j = 1\right\},
$${#eq-Pi-definition}
the $(J-1)$-sphere of radius $\sqrt{\hat{\psi}}$ centered at the origin,
$$
\mathcal{S}_{\hat{\psi}} = \left\{ \symbf{x} \in \mathbbm{R}^J: \|\symbf{x}\|^2 = \hat{\psi} \right\},
$${#eq-S-psi-hat-definition}
and their intersection
$$
\mathcal{L}_{\hat{\psi}} = \Pi \cap \mathcal{S}_{\hat{\psi}}.
$${#eq-L-psi-hat-definition}
Note that $\Delta^{J-1} \subset \Pi$. Therefore
$$
\begin{aligned}
\Omega_{\hat{\psi}}
&= \left\{\symbf{\theta} \in \Delta^{J-1} : \|\symbf{\theta}\|^2 = \hat{\psi}\right\} &&\eqref{eq-omega-hat-psi-simpson} \\
&= \Delta^{J-1} \cap \mathcal{S}_{\hat{\psi}} &&\eqref{eq-S-psi-hat-definition}\\
&= \Delta^{J-1} \cap \Pi \cap \mathcal{S}_{\hat{\psi}} &&(\text{since } \Delta^{J-1} \subset \Pi) \\
&= \Delta^{J-1} \cap \mathcal{L}_{\hat{\psi}}, &&\eqref{eq-L-psi-hat-definition}
\end{aligned}
$$
so $\Omega_{\hat{\psi}} = \mathcal{L}_{\hat{\psi}}$ if and only if $\mathcal{L}_{\hat{\psi}} \subset \Delta^{J-1}$.

To build intuition for the general case, consider $J = 3$. Here $\Pi$ is the plane through $(1,0,0)$, $(0,1,0)$, and $(0,0,1)$, and $\Delta^2$ is the triangle with those vertices. The set $\mathcal{S}_{\hat{\psi}}$ is a sphere of radius
$\sqrt{\hat{\psi}}$ centered at the origin, and $\mathcal{L}_{\hat{\psi}}$ is the circle formed by its intersection with $\Pi$. As $\hat{\psi}$ grows the circle expands, remaining entirely inside $\Delta^2$ for small values of $\hat{\psi}$ and
eventually clipping through its edges. When clipping occurs, $\Omega_{\hat{\psi}}$ is no longer the full circle but the arcs of $\mathcal{L}_{\hat{\psi}}$ that remain inside $\Delta^2$ (see \autoref{fig:simplex-level-sets} in Section \ref{sec-J=3}). Whether and when clipping occurs depends on $\hat{\psi}$ and $J$, as derived in Section \ref{sec-clipping-threshold}.

We may write any $\symbf{x} \in \Pi$ as $\symbf{x} = \mathbf{c} + \mathbf{v}$, where $\mathbf{c} = (1/J)\mathbf{1}$ is the vector extending from the origin to the centroid of $\Delta^{J-1}$, and $\mathbf{v} = \symbf{x} - \mathbf{c}$ is the
displacement vector extending from the centroid to $\symbf{x}$. Since
$$
\mathbf{1} \cdot \mathbf{v} = \sum_{j=1}^J v_j = \sum_{j=1}^J (x_j - c_j) =
\sum_{j=1}^J x_j - \sum_{j=1}^J c_j = 1 - 1 = 0,
$$
$\mathbf{v}$ is orthogonal to $\mathbf{1}$ and hence to $\mathbf{c}$. Now suppose $\mathbf{x} \in \mathcal{L}_{\hat{\psi}}$, so it further satisfies $\|\symbf{x}\|^2 = \hat{\psi}$. Expanding,
$$
\|\symbf{x}\|^2 = \|\mathbf{c} + \mathbf{v}\|^2
= \underbrace{\|\mathbf{c}\|^2}_{1/J} + \underbrace{2\mathbf{c}\cdot\mathbf{v}}_{0} +
\|\mathbf{v}\|^2
= \frac{1}{J} + \|\mathbf{v}\|^2
= \hat{\psi},
$$
so $\|\mathbf{v}\|^2 = \hat{\psi} - 1/J$. Every point in $\mathcal{L}_{\hat{\psi}}$ therefore lies at a distance
$$
r(\hat{\psi}, J) = \sqrt{\hat{\psi} - \frac{1}{J}}
$${#eq-r-definition}
from $\mathbf{c}$, so $\mathcal{L}_{\hat{\psi}}$ is a $(J-2)$-sphere of radius $r(\hat{\psi}, J)$ centered at $\mathbf{c}$ within $\Pi$, degenerating to the single point $\mathbf{c}$ only when $\hat{\psi} = 1/J$, i.e.\ when the observed counts are exactly equal across all categories.

\subsubsection{The Clipping Threshold} \label{sec-clipping-threshold}

The facets of $\Delta^{J-1}$ are its $(J-2)$-dimensional faces, each consisting of all points with one coordinate equal to zero. Each facet is uniquely identified by the vertex opposite to it, so there are exactly $J$ facets in total. Since swapping two vertices also swaps the corresponding two facets while leaving all others unchanged, and any such swap can be achieved by a permutation of coordinates that leaves $\mathbf{c} = (1/J)\mathbf{1}$ unchanged, the distance from $\mathbf{c}$ to any one facet equals the distance to any other. This common distance is called the inradius of $\Delta^{J-1}$, and the shape of $\Omega_{\hat{\psi}}$ depends on whether $r(\hat{\psi}, J)$ exceeds it.

To compute the inradius, we need the closest point on a facet to $\mathbf{c}$. By the same  coordinate-swap argument, any two points within a given facet that are related by a permutation of the non-zero coordinates must be equidistant from $\mathbf{c}$, so the closest point must be invariant under all such permutations. Consequently, all of its non-zero coordinates must be equal. For the facet opposite $\symbf{e}_1$, consisting of all points in $\Delta^{J-1}$ with first coordinate equal to zero, this closest point is the facet centroid $\mathbf{p} = (0, 1/(J-1), \ldots, 1/(J-1))$.

The inradius is therefore
$$
r_{\mathrm{in}} = \|\mathbf{c} - \mathbf{p}\| = \left\|\left(\frac{1}{J},\,
\frac{-1}{J(J-1)},\, \ldots,\, \frac{-1}{J(J-1)}\right)\right\| =
\sqrt{\frac{1}{J^2} + \frac{J-1}{J^2(J-1)^2}} = \sqrt{\frac{1}{J(J-1)}}.
$$
Setting $r(\hat{\psi}, J) = r_{\mathrm{in}}$ gives the clipping threshold $\hat{\psi} = 1/(J-1)$. When $\hat{\psi} < 1/(J-1)$, $\mathcal{L}_{\hat{\psi}}$ lies entirely within $\Delta^{J-1}$, and $\Omega_{\hat{\psi}} = \mathcal{L}_{\hat{\psi}}$ is a complete $(J-2)$-sphere. At $\hat{\psi} = 1/(J-1)$, $\mathcal{L}_{\hat{\psi}}$ is simultaneously tangent to all $J$ facets, touching at $(1/(J-1), \ldots, 1/(J-1), 0)$ and its permutations. When $\hat{\psi} > 1/(J-1)$, $\mathcal{L}_{\hat{\psi}}$ clips through all $J$ facets, and $\Omega_{\hat{\psi}} \subset \mathcal{L}_{\hat{\psi}}$, breaking into $J$ disconnected but identical spherical caps, one near each vertex. We will refer to the cases where $\Omega_{\hat{\psi}} = \mathcal{L}_{\hat{\psi}}$ and $\Omega_{\hat{\psi}} \subset \mathcal{L}_{\hat{\psi}}$ as the connected and disconnected regimes, respectively.

\subsubsection{Cap Geometry} \label{sec-cap-geometry}

Suppose we are in the disconnected regime. Let $\mathcal{C}_j$ denote the cap near vertex $\symbf{e}_j$, so that
$$
\Omega_{\hat{\psi}} = \bigcup_{j=1}^J \mathcal{C}_j.
$${#eq-omega-psi-hat-union}
For a point $\symbf{\omega} = (\omega_1, \ldots, \omega_J) \in \mathcal{C}_j$, the coordinate $\omega_j$ is strictly larger than all others, reflecting the proximity of the cap to $\symbf{e}_j$. We will refer to $\omega_j$ as the dominant coordinate and $\omega_k$ for $k \neq j$ as the non-dominant coordinates. Since $\omega_j > \omega_k$ for all $k \neq j$ and $\sum_{k=1}^J \omega_k = 1$, it follows that $J\omega_j > 1$ and hence $\omega_j > 1/J$. 

The cap axis of $\mathcal{C}_j$ is the line segment from $\mathbf{c}$ to $\symbf{e}_j$, with unit direction
$$
\mathbf{n}_j = \frac{\symbf{e}_j - \mathbf{c}}{\|\symbf{e}_j - \mathbf{c}\|}.
$${#eq-cap-axis-vector}
The cap center is the point where the cap axis intersects $\mathcal{C}_j$. A boundary point of $\mathcal{C}_j$ is any point in $\mathcal{C}_j$ that lies on a facet of $\Delta^{J-1}$, i.e. where one of the non-dominant coordinates equals zero. The angular radius $\alpha$ of $\mathcal{C}_j$ is the angle at $\mathbf{c}$ between the cap axis and the direction to any boundary point $\mathbf{b}$ of $\mathcal{C}_j$. 

Since $\mathbf{n}_j$ is a unit vector and $\mathbf{b} \in \mathcal{L}_{\hat{\psi}}$ lies at a distance $r(\hat{\psi}, J)$ from $\mathbf{c}$ (see @eq-r-definition), $\alpha$ satisfies
$$
\mathbf{n}_j \cdot (\mathbf{b} - \mathbf{c}) = r\cos\alpha,
$$
and therefore
$$
\alpha = \arccos\!\left(\frac{\mathbf{n}_j \cdot (\mathbf{b} -
\mathbf{c})}{r}\right).
$${#eq-angular-radius}
By the symmetry established above, $\alpha$ is the same for all $J$ caps and all boundary points of each cap, so it suffices to compute $\alpha$ for any boundary point of $\mathcal{C}_1$. Since $\alpha$ completely characterizes the extent of each cap, its computation as a function of $\hat{\psi}$ and $J$ is a prerequisite for the sampling procedure developed in Section \ref{sec-disconnected-regime-sampling}.

Of the $J$ facets of $\Delta^{J-1}$, $\mathcal{C}_1$ is bounded by the $J-1$ on which one of the non-dominant coordinates $\omega_2, \ldots, \omega_J$ vanishes. Each boundary point therefore has $\omega_1 > 1/J$, exactly one of $\omega_2, \ldots, \omega_J$ equal to zero, and the remaining $J-2$ strictly positive. Without loss of generality, take the boundary point where $\omega_2 = 0$. Since $\alpha$ is the same for all boundary points, we may seek a representative of symmetric form with $\omega_3 = \cdots = \omega_J = a$ for some $a > 0$, and verify its existence by solving the resulting system explicitly.

Set $\omega_2 = 0$ and $\omega_3 = \cdots = \omega_J = a$. Since $\symbf{\omega} \in \mathcal{L}_{\hat{\psi}}$, the two constraints defining $\mathcal{L}_{\hat{\psi}}$ give
$$
\omega_1 + (J-2)a = 1
$${#eq-omega_1-constraint-1}
and
$$
\omega_1^2 + (J-2)a^2 = \hat{\psi}.
$${#eq-omega_1-constraint-2}
Since $\omega_1$ is the dominant coordinate, $a < \omega_1$. Substituting into @eq-omega_1-constraint-1 gives
$$
1 = \omega_1 + (J-2)a > a + (J-2)a = (J-1)a,
$$
and hence
$$
a < \frac{1}{J-1}.
$${#eq-a-upper-bound}
substituting $\omega_1 = 1 - (J-2)a$ from @eq-omega_1-constraint-1 into @eq-omega_1-constraint-2 and rearranging yields the quadratic
$$
(J-2)(J-1)a^2 - 2(J-2)a + (1-\hat{\psi}) = 0,
$$
whose roots are
$$
\frac{1 - \sqrt{\frac{(J-1)\hat{\psi} - 1}{J-2}}}{J-1} \quad \text{and} \quad
\frac{1 + \sqrt{\frac{(J-1)\hat{\psi} - 1}{J-2}}}{J-1}.
$$
Both roots are real for $\hat{\psi} \geq 1/(J-1)$, confirming the existence of the symmetric boundary point. Only the smaller root satisfies @eq-a-upper-bound, so
$$
a = \frac{1 - \sqrt{\frac{(J-1)\hat{\psi} - 1}{J-2}}}{J-1}.
$${#eq-quadratic-solution}

It remains to evaluate @eq-angular-radius at $\mathbf{b} = (\omega_1, 0, a, \ldots, a)$. We first compute $\mathbf{n}_1$ from @eq-cap-axis-vector. The vector $\mathbf{e}_1 - \mathbf{c}$ has components
$$
\begin{aligned}
\mathbf{e}_1 - \mathbf{c}
&= (1, 0, \ldots, 0) - \left( \frac{1}{J}, \ldots, \frac{1}{J} \right) \\
&= \left( \frac{J-1}{J}, -\frac{1}{J}, \ldots, -\frac{1}{J} \right) \\
&= \frac{1}{J} \Big(J-1, \underbrace{-1, \ldots, -1}_{J-1}\Big),
\end{aligned}
$$
with norm
$$
\begin{aligned}
\| \mathbf{e}_1 - \mathbf{c} \|
&= \frac{1}{J} \sqrt{ (J-1)^2 + \sum_{j=1}^{J-1} (-1)^2 } \\
&= \frac{1}{J} \sqrt{ (J-1)^2 + (J-1) } \\
&= \frac{1}{J} \sqrt{ J(J-1) } \\
&= \sqrt{ \frac{J-1}{J} },
\end{aligned}
$$
and hence
$$
\symbf{n}_1
= \frac{\symbf{e}_1 - \mathbf{c}}{\|\symbf{e}_1 - \mathbf{c}\|}
= \frac{\frac{1}{J} (J-1, -1, \ldots, -1)}{\sqrt{ \frac{J-1}{J} }}
= \frac{1}{\sqrt{J(J-1)}}(J-1, -1, \ldots, -1).
$$
The displacement $\mathbf{b} - \mathbf{c}$ has components
$$
\mathbf{b} - \mathbf{c}
= ( \omega_1, 0, a, \ldots, a ) - \left( \frac{1}{J}, \ldots, \frac{1}{J} \right)
= \bigg( \omega_1 - \frac{1}{J},\ -\frac{1}{J},\ \underbrace{a - \frac{1}{J},
\ldots, a - \frac{1}{J}}_{J-2}\bigg).
$$
Taking the dot product,
$$
\begin{aligned}
\mathbf{n}_1 \cdot (\mathbf{b} - \mathbf{c})
&= \frac{1}{\sqrt{J(J-1)}}(J-1, -1, \ldots, -1) \cdot \left( \omega_1 -
\frac{1}{J},\ -\frac{1}{J},\ a - \frac{1}{J},\ \ldots,\ a - \frac{1}{J} \right) \\
&= \frac{(J-1)\left( \omega_1 - \frac{1}{J} \right) + \frac{1}{J} - (J-2)\left(
a-\frac{1}{J} \right)}{\sqrt{J(J-1)}} \\
&= \frac{(J-1)\omega_1 - (J-2)a - \frac{J-2}{J} + \frac{J-2}{J}}{\sqrt{J(J-1)}} \\
&= \frac{(J-1)\omega_1 - (J-2)a}{\sqrt{J(J-1)}}.
\end{aligned}
$$
Substituting $\omega_1 = 1 - (J-2)a$ and $a$ as in @eq-quadratic-solution, the
numerator simplifies to
$$
\begin{aligned}
(J-1)\omega_1 - (J-2)a
&= (J-1) \left[ 1 - (J-2)a \right] - (J-2)a \\
&= (J-1) - J(J-2)a \\
&= (J-1) - J(J-2) \left[ \frac{1 - \sqrt{\frac{(J-1)\hat{\psi} - 1}{J-2}}}{J-1}
\right] \\
&= \frac{(J-1)^2 - J(J-2)}{J-1} + \frac{J\sqrt{(J-2) \left( (J-1)\hat{\psi} - 1
\right)}}{J-1} \\
&= \frac{1 + J\sqrt{(J-2)\bigl((J-1)\hat{\psi}-1\bigr)}}{J-1},
\end{aligned}
$$
where we used $(J-1)^2 - J(J-2) = 1$. Dividing by $r(\hat{\psi}, J)$ and using $\sqrt{J(J-1)} \cdot \sqrt{\hat{\psi} - 1/J} = \sqrt{(J-1)(J\hat{\psi}-1)}$, we have
$$
\frac{1}{r(\hat{\psi}, J)}\,\mathbf{n}_1 \cdot (\mathbf{b} - \mathbf{c})
= \frac{1}{\sqrt{\hat{\psi} - \frac{1}{J}}} \cdot
\frac{\frac{1 + J\sqrt{(J-2)\bigl((J-1)\hat{\psi}-1\bigr)}}{J-1}}{\sqrt{J(J-1)}}
= \frac{1 + J\sqrt{(J-2)\bigl((J-1)\hat{\psi}-1\bigr)}}{(J-1)\sqrt{(J-1)(J\hat{\psi}
- 1)}}.
$$
Substituting into @eq-angular-radius gives the angular radius
$$
\alpha(\hat{\psi}, J) = \arccos\!\left(
  \frac{1 + J\sqrt{(J-2)\bigl((J-1)\hat{\psi}-1\bigr)}}{(J-1)\sqrt{(J-1)(J\hat{\psi}-1)}}
\right), \qquad \hat{\psi} \in \left[\frac{1}{J-1}, 1\right).
$${#eq-alpha-psi-hat-general}
At $\hat{\psi} = 1/(J-1)$, $\alpha = \arccos(1/(J-1))$; as $\hat{\psi} \to 1$, $\alpha \to 0$ and each cap collapses to its vertex.

\subsubsection{Permutation Symmetry and Monte Carlo Sampling} \label{sec-permutation-symmetry}

The symmetric group $S_J$ acts on $\Omega_{\hat{\psi}}$ by permuting category labels. The orbit of a point $\symbf{\omega} \in \Omega_{\hat{\psi}}$ under this action is the set $\{\sigma(\symbf{\omega}) : \sigma \in S_J\}$ of all points reachable by permuting the coordinates of $\symbf{\omega}$. The $J!$ elements of $S_J$ decompose into two types: those that change the dominant coordinate, mapping the cap near $\symbf{e}_j$ to the cap near $\symbf{e}_k$ for $j \neq k$, and for each cap, the $(J-1)!$ permutations of the non-dominant coordinates that fix the dominant coordinate and map the cap onto itself by reflecting it about the axis from $\mathbf{c}$ to its corresponding vertex. This gives $J \times (J-1)! = J!$ total permutations, consistent with $|S_J|$. 

The orbit size depends on how many within-cap permutations fix $\symbf{\omega}$. For a generic point with all non-dominant coordinates distinct, none do, and the orbit has $J!$ elements with $(J-1)!$ in each cap. Partially degenerate points, where some but not all non-dominant coordinates coincide, have smaller orbits. Fully degenerate points with all non-dominant coordinates equal are fixed by all $(J-1)!$ within-cap permutations, giving orbits of size $J$. These degenerate cases form a set of measure zero in $\Omega_{\hat{\psi}}$ and do not affect the Monte Carlo approximation in practice.

We can exploit the orbit structure of $S_J$ to obtain equivalent coverage of $\Omega_{\hat{\psi}}$ at a fraction of the cost. Rather than drawing $J! \cdot R$ points independently from $\Omega_{\hat{\psi}}$, we instead sample $R$ independent base points from a single cap and expand each to its full orbit of $J!$ by applying all elements of $S_J$. The within-orbit expansion is deterministic, so the Monte Carlo variance is driven entirely by the $R$ independent base draws. Exact coverage of all $J$ caps is guaranteed for every orbit, reducing variance relative to naive independent sampling. This procedure applies in both regimes: when $\hat{\psi} \geq 1/(J-1)$ the caps are geometrically separated by the simplex boundary, and when $\hat{\psi} < 1/(J-1)$ the $J$-fold symmetry of $S_J$ still partitions $\mathcal{L}_{\hat{\psi}}$ into $J$ equal sectors, one associated with each vertex, and the sampling strategy is identical. The resulting approximation is
$$
\bar{L}(\psi) \approx \frac{1}{J!\, R} \sum_{i=1}^{R} \sum_{\sigma \in S_J}
L\!\left(b\!\left(\sigma(\symbf{\omega}^{(i)}), \psi;\, \hat{\psi}\right)\right),
$${#eq-IL-simpson-general}
where $\symbf{\omega}^{(1)}, \ldots, \symbf{\omega}^{(R)}$ are drawn independently from a single cap, and $b(\symbf{\omega}, \psi;\, \hat{\psi})$ denotes the maximizer of $\sum_j \omega_j \log \theta_j$ with respect to $\symbf{\theta} \in \Delta^{J-1}$ subject to $D(\symbf{\theta}) = \psi$.  In the connected regime, $\mathbf{u}$ is drawn uniformly on the
$(J-2)$-sphere of radius $r(\hat{\psi}, J)$. In the disconnected regime, each base point is obtained by uniformly sampling a direction within angular distance $\alpha(\hat{\psi}, J)$ of the cap axis $\mathbf{n}_1$ (see @eq-cap-axis-vector and @eq-alpha-psi-hat-general) and setting $\mathbf{u} = \mathbf{c} + r(\hat{\psi}, J)\mathbf{u}$ for the sampled unit direction $\mathbf{v}$.

\subsubsection{Sampling in the Connected Regime} \label{sec-connected-regime-sampling}

In the connected regime, $\Omega_{\hat{\psi}} = \mathcal{L}_{\hat{\psi}}$ by definition, and sampling uniformly from $\Omega_{\hat{\psi}}$ reduces to sampling uniformly from the full $(J-2)$-sphere of radius $r(\hat{\psi}, J)$ (see @eq-r-definition) centered at $\mathbf{c}$ within $\Pi$. To do so, we may draw $\mathbf{z} \sim \mathcal{N}(\mathbf{0}, \mathbf{I}_J)$ and project it onto $\mathbf{1}^\perp = \{\mathbf{v} \in \mathbbm{R}^J : \mathbf{1} \cdot \mathbf{v} = 0\}$ by subtracting its mean,
$$
\mathbf{z}' = \mathbf{z} - \bar{z}\mathbf{1}, \qquad \bar{z} =
\frac{1}{J}\sum_{j=1}^J z_j,
$$
so that $\mathbf{1} \cdot \mathbf{z}' = 0$. Since $\mathbf{z}'$ lies in $\mathbf{1}^\perp$ by construction, the relevant notion of symmetry is invariance under rotations that map $\mathbf{1}^\perp$ to itself. Such invariance implies that no direction within $\mathbf{1}^\perp$ is preferred over any other, so $\mathbf{z}' / \|\mathbf{z}'\|$ is uniform on the unit $(J-2)$-sphere within $\mathbf{1}^\perp$. This is precisely the property needed to ensure that a point $\mathbf{u} = \mathbf{c} + r \cdot \mathbf{z}' / \|\mathbf{z}'\|$ is uniform on $\mathcal{L}_{\hat{\psi}}$. It therefore suffices to show that the distribution of $\mathbf{z}'$ is invariant under all rotations that map $\mathbf{1}^\perp$ to itself.

Let $\mathbf{Q}$ be a rotation matrix — an orthogonal matrix with determinant $+1$ — that maps $\mathbf{1}^\perp$ to itself. The orthogonality of $\mathbf{Q}$ implies that it preserves inner products, 
$$
\langle \mathbf{Q}\mathbf{u}, \mathbf{Q}\mathbf{v}\rangle = \mathbf{u}^\top
\mathbf{Q}^\top \mathbf{Q}\mathbf{v} = \mathbf{u}^\top\mathbf{v} =
\langle \mathbf{u}, \mathbf{v} \rangle,
$$
for any $\mathbf{u}, \mathbf{v} \in \mathbbm{R}^J$. Therefore, if $\mathbf{1}$ is orthogonal to some $\mathbf{v} \in \mathbf{1}^\perp$, then
$$
\langle\mathbf{1}, \mathbf{v} \rangle = 0 \implies \langle \mathbf{Q}\mathbf{1},
\mathbf{Q}\mathbf{v} \rangle = 0,
$$
so $\mathbf{Q}\mathbf{1}$ is orthogonal to $\mathbf{Q}\mathbf{v}$. Since $\mathbf{Q}$ maps $\mathbf{1}^\perp$ to itself, $\mathbf{Q}\mathbf{v} \in \mathbf{1}^\perp$ for any $\mathbf{v} \in \mathbf{1}^\perp$. As $\mathbf{v}$ was arbitrary, $\mathbf{Q}\mathbf{1}$ must be orthogonal to every vector in $\mathbf{1}^\perp$, so $\mathbf{Q}\mathbf{1} \in \mathrm{span}(\mathbf{1})$, i.e. $\mathbf{Q}\mathbf{1} = k \mathbf{1}$ for some scalar $k$. Rotation matrices preserve norms, so
$\|\mathbf{Q}\mathbf{1}\| = \|\mathbf{1}\|$, implying $|k| = 1$. The determinant $+1$ condition then forces $k = 1$, so $\mathbf{Q}\mathbf{1} = \mathbf{1}$. Applying $\mathbf{Q}^{-1}$ to both sides gives $\mathbf{Q}^{-1} \mathbf{1} = \mathbf{1}$, and since $\mathbf{Q}^\top = \mathbf{Q}^{-1}$ by orthogonality, we have $\mathbf{Q}^\top\mathbf{1} = \mathbf{1}$.
The sample mean of $\mathbf{Q}\mathbf{z}$ therefore satisfies $\overline{\mathbf{Q}\mathbf{z}} = \frac{1}{J}\mathbf{1}^\top \mathbf{Q}\mathbf{z} = \frac{1}{J}(\mathbf{Q}^\top\mathbf{1})^\top\mathbf{z} = \frac{1}{J}\mathbf{1}^\top\mathbf{z}= \bar{z}$,
so
$$
\mathrm{proj}_{\mathbf{1}^\perp}(\mathbf{Q}\mathbf{z}) = \mathbf{Q}\mathbf{z} - \bar{z}\mathbf{1} = \mathbf{Q}\mathbf{z} - \bar{z}\mathbf{Q}\mathbf{1} = \mathbf{Q}(\mathbf{z} - \bar{z}\mathbf{1}) = \mathbf{Q}\mathbf{z}' = \mathbf{Q}\mathrm{proj}_{\mathbf{1}^\perp}(\mathbf{z})
$$
That is, projection onto $\mathbf{1}^\perp$ and rotation within it commute. Note that $\mathbf{Q}\mathbf{z} \overset{d}{=} \mathbf{z}$ since $\mathbf{Q}\mathbf{z} \sim \mathcal{N}(\mathbf{0}, \mathbf{Q}\mathbf{Q}^\top) = \mathcal{N}(\mathbf{0}, \mathbf{I}_J)$. Therefore, we have
$$
\mathbf{Q}\mathbf{z}' = \mathbf{Q} \mathrm{proj}_{\mathbf{1}^\perp}(\mathbf{z}) = \mathrm{proj}_{\mathbf{1}^\perp}(\mathbf{Q} \mathbf{z}) \overset{d}{=} \mathrm{proj}_{\mathbf{1}^\perp}(\mathbf{z}) = \mathbf{z}',
$$
so $\mathbf{Q}\mathbf{z}' \overset{d}{=} \mathbf{z}'$.

Thus, the distribution of $\mathbf{z}'$ is invariant under any rotation that maps $\mathbf{1}^\perp$ to itself. A random vector with this property must assign equal probability to all directions within $\mathbf{1}^\perp$, since any two directions can be mapped to one another by such a rotation. It follows that $\mathbf{z}' / \|\mathbf{z}'\|$ is distributed uniformly on the unit $(J-2)$-sphere within $\mathbf{1}^\perp$. Rescaling by $r$ gives a vector $\mathbf{v} = r \cdot \mathbf{z}' / \|\mathbf{z}'\|$ that is uniform on the $(J-2)$-sphere of radius $r$ within $\mathbf{1}^\perp$, meaning all points at distance $r$ from the origin in $\mathbf{1}^\perp$ are equally likely. Translating by $\mathbf{c}$ shifts the center of this $(J-2)$-sphere from the origin to $\mathbf{c}$, giving a point $\mathbf{x} = \mathbf{c} + \mathbf{v}$ that is uniform on the $(J-2)$-sphere of radius $r$ centered at $\mathbf{c}$ within the affine subspace $\mathbf{c} + \mathbf{1}^\perp = \Pi$. This is precisely $\mathcal{L}_{\hat{\psi}}$ (see @eq-L-psi-hat-definition and @eq-r-definition). Hence, to sample a point uniformly at random from $\Omega_{\hat{\psi}}$ in the connected regime, we need merely to draw $\mathbf{z} \sim \mathcal{N}(\mathbf{0}, \mathbf{I}_J)$, project onto $\mathbf{1}^\perp$ by setting $\mathbf{z}' = \mathbf{z} - \bar{z}\mathbf{1}$, and calculate $\mathbf{u} = \mathbf{c} + r \cdot \mathbf{z}' / \|\mathbf{z}'\|$.

\subsubsection{Sampling in the Disconnected Regime} \label{sec-disconnected-regime-sampling}

For $J \geq 3$, the disconnected regime arises when $\hat{\psi} \geq 1/(J-1)$, and $\Omega_{\hat{\psi}}$ consists of $J$ disjoint spherical caps, one near each vertex of $\Delta^{J-1}$. We need not consider $J=2$ here since, as shown in Section \ref{sec-J=2}, it is impossible for the disconnected regime to arise in such a case. By the permutation symmetry of $\Omega_{\hat{\psi}}$ under $S_J$, all $J$ caps are geometrically identical, so without loss of generality we may describe how to sample only from $\mathcal{C}_1$, the cap near $\symbf{e}_1$.

Any point $\mathbf{p} \in \mathcal{C}_1$ lies in $\Pi$ and can be written as $\mathbf{p} = \mathbf{c} + \mathbf{d}$, where $\mathbf{d}$ is the displacement from the centroid to $\mathbf{p}$. Since $\Pi = \mathbf{c} + \mathbf{1}^\perp$ is an affine subspace with $\sum_j p_j = 1$ for all $\mathbf{p} \in \Pi$, the difference between any two points in $\Pi$ sums to zero and therefore lies in $\mathbf{1}^\perp$. So $\mathbf{d} = \mathbf{p} - \mathbf{c}$ lies in $\mathbf{1}^\perp$ and has length $r = r(\hat{\psi}, J)$ (see @eq-r-definition).

Any vector in $\mathbf{1}^\perp$ can be decomposed into the sum of two components, one pointing along a chosen reference direction and one that is orthogonal to it. The natural reference direction here is $\mathbf{n}_1$, the unit vector from $\mathbf{c}$ toward $\symbf{e}_1$. Like $\mathbf{d}$, this vector lies in $\mathbf{1}^\perp$, since it is proportional to $\symbf{e}_1 - \mathbf{c}$, the difference between two points in $\Pi$. Writing $\gamma$ for the angle between $\mathbf{d}$ and $\mathbf{n}_1$ and $h = \cos\gamma$, the component of $\mathbf{d}$ pointing along $\mathbf{n}_1$ has length $rh$, and the component orthogonal to $\mathbf{n}_1$ has length $r\sqrt{1-h^2}$. When $J = 3$ the subspace of $\mathbf{1}^\perp$ orthogonal to $\mathbf{n}_1$ is zero-dimensional, so the orthogonal component has a fixed direction and the displacement $\mathbf{d}$ is fully determined by $h$ alone. For $J \geq 4$ this subspace has dimension $J - 3 \geq 1$; letting $\mathbf{u}$ denote a unit vector within it, the decomposition is
$$
\mathbf{d} = rh\,\mathbf{n}_1 + r\sqrt{1-h^2}\,\mathbf{u} =
r\!\left(h\,\mathbf{n}_1 + \sqrt{1-h^2}\,\mathbf{u}\right).
$${#eq-cap-decomposition}

The scalar $h$ controls how far along the cap axis the point $\mathbf{p}$ lies. When $h = 1$ the displacement points directly along the cap axis, placing $\mathbf{p}$ at the tip of the cap, the point nearest to $\symbf{e_1}$. When $h = \cos\alpha$ the displacement makes the maximum angle $\alpha$ with the axis, placing $\mathbf{p}$ at one of the boundaries of the cap. For $J \geq 4$, a point on $\mathcal{C}_1$ is fully specified by the pair $(h, \mathbf{u})$, which separately control how far the point is from the tip of the cap and in which direction around the cap axis it lies.

To sample $\symbf{p}$ uniformly from $\mathcal{C}_1$ when $J \geq 4$, it suffices to draw $h$ and $\mathbf{u}$ independently from their respective marginal distributions, since the decomposition in @eq-cap-decomposition separates the two degrees of freedom. The component $\mathbf{u}$ is sampled by the same Gaussian projection used in the connected regime, extended to project out both the $\mathbf{1}$ direction and the $\mathbf{n}_1$ direction before normalizing: draw $\mathbf{z} \sim \mathcal{N}(\mathbf{0}, \mathbf{I}_J)$, subtract its mean to project onto $\mathbf{1}^\perp$, then subtract the component along $\mathbf{n}_1$, and normalize. By the same rotational symmetry argument as in the connected regime, the result is uniform on the unit $(J-3)$-sphere within the orthogonal subspace. When $J = 3$, the orthogonal subspace is one-dimensional, so the unit $(J-3)$-sphere within it is zero-dimensional, consisting of just two points $\pm\mathbf{u}_0$ for a fixed unit vector $\mathbf{u}_0$, and all randomness in the draw comes from $h$.

Sampling $h$ requires the marginal density of $\gamma$. Consider the latitude ring at angle $\gamma$ from the cap axis, defined as the set of all points on $\mathcal{C}_1$ at angle $\gamma$ relative to $\mathbf{n}_1$. From the decomposition @eq-cap-decomposition, fixing $\gamma$ fixes the component of $\mathbf{d}$ along $\mathbf{n}_1$ to $r\cos\gamma$, while the orthogonal component is free to point in any direction $\mathbf{u}$ within the $(J-3)$-dimensional subspace orthogonal to $\mathbf{n}_1$, at a fixed distance $r\sin\gamma$ from the axis. The latitude ring is therefore a $(J-3)$-sphere of radius $r\sin\gamma$. Since the surface area of a $k$-sphere of radius $\rho$ scales as $\rho^k$, the surface area of this ring is proportional to $(r\sin\gamma)^{J-3}$. The surface element of $\mathcal{L}_{\hat{\psi}}$ at angle $\gamma$ therefore decomposes as the product of the area of the latitude ring and the arc length width of an infinitesimal band around it,
$$
dA \propto (r\sin\gamma)^{J-3} \cdot r d\gamma.
$$

Under a uniform distribution on $\mathcal{C}_1$, the probability of landing in an infinitesimal band between $\gamma$ and $\gamma + d\gamma$ is proportional to the surface area of that band. Since the uniform density is constant across the band, integrating it over all directions $\mathbf{u}$ within the latitude ring simply yields the surface area of the ring, which is proportional to $(r\sin\gamma)^{J-3}$. The probability of landing in the band is therefore
$$
f(\gamma) d\gamma \propto (r\sin\gamma)^{J-3} \cdot r d\gamma.
$$
Dividing through by $d\gamma$ and absorbing the constant factors of $r$ into the proportionality gives the marginal density of $\gamma$,
$$
f(\gamma) \propto \sin(\gamma)^{J-3}, \qquad \gamma \in [0, \alpha].
$${#eq-gamma-marginal}

For $J = 3$ the exponent vanishes so $f(\gamma) \propto 1$, meaning $\gamma$ is uniform on $[0, \alpha]$ and $h = \cos(U\alpha)$ for $U \sim \mathrm{Uniform}(0, 1)$ suffices. For $J \geq 4$ the density @eq-gamma-marginal has no closed-form CDF in general, but the substitution $s = \sin^2\gamma$ transforms it into a recognizable family. Differentiating gives $ds = 2\sin\gamma\cos\gamma\,d\gamma$, so $d\gamma = ds / (2\sqrt{s}\sqrt{1-s})$, and substituting into @eq-gamma-marginal yields the density of $s$,
$$
\begin{aligned}
f_s(s) 
&= f(\gamma) \cdot \left|\frac{d\gamma}{ds}\right| \\
&\propto \sin(\gamma)^{J-3} \cdot \frac{1}{2\sqrt{s}\sqrt{1-s}} \\
&= s^{(J-3)/2} \cdot \frac{1}{2\sqrt{s}\sqrt{1-s}} \\
&= \frac{1}{2} s^{(J-3)/2 - 1/2}(1-s)^{-1/2} \\
&= \frac{1}{2} s^{(J-2)/2\,-\,1}(1-s)^{1/2\,-\,1},
\qquad s \in \bigl[0,\, \sin^2\!\alpha\bigr].
\end{aligned}
$$
We recognize this as the kernel of a $\mathrm{Beta}((J-2)/2,\, 1/2)$ distribution truncated to $[0, \sin^2\!\alpha]$. An exact draw is obtained by inverting the truncated Beta CDF. Draw $U \sim \mathrm{Uniform}(0, 1)$, compute
$$
q = U \cdot I_{\sin^2\!\alpha}\!\left(\tfrac{J-2}{2},\, \tfrac{1}{2}\right),
$$
where $I_x(a, b)$ denotes the regularized incomplete beta function, and set
$$
s = I^{-1}_{q}\!\left(\tfrac{J-2}{2},\, \tfrac{1}{2}\right).
$${#eq-beta-inversion}
Scaling $U$ by $I_{\sin^2\!\alpha}((J-2)/2, 1/2)$ before inversion restricts the draw to $[0, \sin^2\!\alpha]$, enforcing the truncation. The height coordinate is then recovered as $h = \sqrt{1 - s}$. This approach is exact and numerically stable for any cap width, including the narrow caps that arise when $\hat{\psi}$ is large and $\alpha$ is small.

In summary, to sample a point uniformly at random from $\mathcal{C}_1$, start by drawing $U \sim \mathrm{Uniform}(0, 1)$ and then proceeding according to the value of $J$. For $J = 3$, set $h = \cos(U\alpha)$, draw $\epsilon \in \{-1, +1\}$ with equal probability, and calculate $\mathbf{p} = \mathbf{c} + r(h\,\mathbf{n}_1 + \sqrt{1-h^2}\,\epsilon\mathbf{u}_0)$, where $\mathbf{u}_0$ is either unit vector orthogonal to $\mathbf{n}_1$ in $\mathbf{1}^\perp$. For $J \geq 4$, compute $q = U \cdot I_{\sin^2\!\alpha}((J-2)/2, 1/2)$, set $s = I^{-1}_q((J-2)/2, 1/2)$, and recover $h = \sqrt{1 - s}$. Then sample $\mathbf{u}$ independently by drawing $\mathbf{z} \sim \mathcal{N}(\mathbf{0}, \mathbf{I}_J)$, subtracting its mean, subtracting the component along $\mathbf{n}_1$, normalizing, and finally calculating $\mathbf{p} = \mathbf{c} + r(h\,\mathbf{n}_1 + \sqrt{1-h^2}\,\mathbf{u})$.

\subsection{The Case $J = 2$} \label{sec-J=2}

When $J = 2$, the simplex $\Delta^1$ is a line segment and $D(\symbf{\theta}) = \theta_1^2 + \theta_2^2 < 1$ for all interior points, so the clipping threshold $1/(J-1) = 1/(2-1) = 1$ is never reached. The disconnected regime therefore never arises, and $\mathcal{L}_{\hat{\psi}}$ degenerates to a $0$-sphere — a pair of points — so $\Omega_{\hat{\psi}}$ consists of exactly two points for any $\hat{\psi} > 1/2$.

The parameter space is $\Delta^1 = \{(\theta_1, \theta_2) : \theta_1 + \theta_2 = 1,\ \theta_1, \theta_2 \in (0,1)\}$, and Simpson's index reduces to 
$$
D(\symbf{\theta}) = \theta_1^2 + (1-\theta_1)^2 = 2\theta_1^2 - 2\theta_1 + 1.
$${#eq-simpson-index-2d}
Setting $D(\symbf{\theta}) = \hat{\psi}$ and solving gives $\theta_1 = (1 \pm \sqrt{2\hat{\psi}-1})/2$, so the two points are
$$
\symbf{\omega}^{(1)} = \left( \frac{1 + \sqrt{2\hat{\psi}-1}}{2},\ \frac{1 -
\sqrt{2\hat{\psi}-1}}{2} \right), \qquad \symbf{\omega}^{(2)} = \left( \frac{1 -
\sqrt{2\hat{\psi}-1}}{2},\ \frac{1 + \sqrt{2\hat{\psi}-1}}{2} \right).
$$
These are the $J = 2$ instances of the $J$ degenerate caps identified in the general case, each collapsing to a single point near one of the two vertices. They are related by the coordinate swap $(\theta_1, \theta_2) \mapsto (\theta_2, \theta_1)$, which is the $J = 2$ instance of the permutation symmetry established above, and migrate toward the corners $(1, 0)$ and $(0, 1)$ as $\hat{\psi} \to 1$. The integrated likelihood at $\psi$ is
$$
\bar{L}(\psi) = L\bigl(b(\symbf{\omega}^{(1)}, \psi;\,
\hat{\psi})\bigr) + L\bigl(b(\symbf{\omega}^{(2)}, \psi;\, \hat{\psi})\bigr),
$${#eq-IL-simpson-2d}
up to a multiplicative constant. Since $\symbf{\omega}^{(1)} = \mathbf{1} - \symbf{\omega}^{(2)}$ and the constraint $D(\symbf{\theta}) = \psi$ is symmetric in $\theta_1$ and $\theta_2$, the maximizer $b(\symbf{\omega}^{(2)}, \psi;\, \hat{\psi})$ is simply $\mathbf{1} - b(\symbf{\omega}^{(1)}, \psi;\, \hat{\psi})$, so only one constrained optimization is needed. The likelihood must still be evaluated separately at each point, however, since $\hat{\psi} > 1/2$ implies $N_1 \neq N_2$, and consequently $L(\symbf{\theta}) = \theta_1^{N_1}\theta_2^{N_2}$ will not be invariant under permutation of $\symbf{\theta}$.

When $\hat{\psi} = 1/2$, the two points coincide at the centroid $\mathbf{c} = (1/2, 1/2)$, which is also the uniform distribution $\hat{\symbf{\theta}} = (1/2, 1/2)$, and $\Omega_{\hat{\psi}} = \{\hat{\symbf{\theta}}\}$. The integrated likelihood then reduces to the single evaluation $L(b(\hat{\symbf{\theta}}, \psi;\, \hat{\psi}))$, which is precisely the profile likelihood maximizer, so the two are identical in this case. More generally, since $\Omega_{\hat{\psi}}$ contains only two points for any $\hat{\psi}$, there is little room for the integrated likelihood to differ from the profile likelihood through averaging over meaningfully distinct nuisance parameters, and the two will tend to agree closely in practice. This is consistent with the well-established result that the integrated likelihood only begins to outperform the profile likelihood when the nuisance parameter is high-dimensional [@berger1999; @DeBin2015].

\subsection{The Case $J = 3$} \label{sec-J=3}

When $J = 3$, $\mathcal{L}_{\hat{\psi}}$ is a circle of radius $r(\hat{\psi}, 3) = \sqrt{\hat{\psi} - 1/3}$ centered at $\mathbf{c}$ within $\Pi$ (see @eq-r-definition). The parameter space $\Delta^2$ is an equilateral triangle, with the facets reducing to three one-dimensional edges. Each edge has length $\sqrt{2}$ and the inradius is $r_{\mathrm{in}} = 1/\sqrt{6}$. The clipping threshold is $1/(J-1) = 1/2$, and the three regimes of the general case become: $\Omega_{\hat{\psi}}$ is a complete circle when $\hat{\psi} < 1/2$, tangent to all three edges at $(1/2, 1/2, 0)$ and its permutations when $\hat{\psi} = 1/2$, and three disjoint arcs when $\hat{\psi} > 1/2$. These are illustrated in \autoref{fig:simplex-level-sets}.

\begin{figure}[H]
  \vspace{-0.8cm}
  \centering
  \includegraphics[width=0.4\textwidth]{files/Images/simplex-level-sets.png}
  \vspace{-0.6cm}
  \caption{%
    \small
    \textsc{Level Sets of Simpson's Index on the Probability Simplex $\Delta^2$.}
    The circle $\mathcal{L}_{\hat{\psi}}$ of radius $r(\hat{\psi}, 3) = \sqrt{\hat{\psi}
    - 1/3}$ centered at the centroid $\mathbf{c}$ and embedded in the affine plane $\Pi$
    is shown for three values of $\hat{\psi}$. When $\hat{\psi} < 1/2$,
    $\mathcal{L}_{\hat{\psi}}$ lies entirely within $\Delta^2$ and $\Omega_{\hat{\psi}}
    = \mathcal{L}_{\hat{\psi}}$ is a complete circle. At $\hat{\psi} = 1/2$,
    $\mathcal{L}_{\hat{\psi}}$ is tangent to all three edges of $\Delta^2$
    simultaneously, touching at the open circles marking the uniform distributions over
    two categories. When $\hat{\psi} > 1/2$, $\mathcal{L}_{\hat{\psi}}$ extends beyond
    $\Delta^2$ and $\Omega_{\hat{\psi}} = \mathcal{L}_{\hat{\psi}} \cap \Delta^2$
    consists of three disjoint arcs, one near each vertex. Each arc subtends an angle
    $2\alpha$ at $\mathbf{c}$, with the centroid-to-vertex line bisecting the arc.
  }
  \vspace{-0.5cm}
  \label{fig:simplex-level-sets}
\end{figure}

Setting $J = 3$ in @eq-alpha-psi-hat-general gives the angular radius of each arc:
$$
\alpha(\hat{\psi}) = \arccos\!\left(
  \frac{1 + 3\sqrt{\hat{\psi} - \tfrac{1}{2}}}{2\sqrt{2\hat{\psi} - 1}}
\right), \qquad \hat{\psi} \in \left[\tfrac{1}{2}, 1\right).
$${#eq-alpha-psi-hat}
At $\hat{\psi} = 1/2$, $\alpha = \pi/3$, so the three arcs tile the full circle, consistent with $\Omega_{\hat{\psi}} = \mathcal{L}_{\hat{\psi}}$ at the threshold. As $\hat{\psi} \to 1$, $\alpha \to 0$ and each arc shrinks to a point at its vertex, consistent with @eq-alpha-psi-hat-general.

Evaluating @eq-IL-simpson-general at $J = 3$ gives $J! = 6$, and the Monte Carlo approximation becomes
$$
\bar{L}(\psi) \approx \frac{1}{6R} \sum_{i=1}^{R} \sum_{\sigma \in S_3}
L\!\left(b\!\left(\sigma(\symbf{\omega}^{(i)}), \psi;\, \hat{\psi}\right)\right),
$${#eq-IL-simpson-3d}
where $\symbf{\omega}^{(1)}, \ldots, \symbf{\omega}^{(R)}$ are drawn independently from a single arc. The six elements of $S_3$ decompose into three cyclic permutations mapping each arc to another, and three reflections mapping each arc onto itself across the axis from $\mathbf{c}$ to its vertex. The transition point $\hat{\psi} = 1/2$ marks the spot where the sector boundaries coincide exactly with the simplex edges.
